notes:
Task and constraints: Find the smallest number on either side of a card that does not appear on both sides of any single card.
Idea: Collect values that are identical on the front and back, then choose the smallest value outside that forbidden set.
Technique and why it applies: A value showing on both sides of one card can never be exposed by flipping that card, so it cannot be the answer. The remaining values are eligible.
Invariant: The set comprehension contains all values forbidden by matching front/back cards.
Edge cases: If no eligible value exists, the code returns zero. It rebuilds the forbidden set inside the list-comprehension condition for every candidate, wasting work.
Complexity: Repeated set construction can lead to O(n²) time; extra storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the smallest good number obtainable by flipping cards, excluding numbers that appear on both sides of the same card.
Idea: Build the forbidden set from cards whose front and back match, then scan both sides for the minimum permitted number.
Technique and why it applies: A matching value cannot be hidden by flipping its card; any other value can be made visible on one side. The scan maintains the smallest eligible candidate.
Invariant: same contains exactly the values that cannot be made good.
Edge cases: If every value is forbidden, the method returns zero. The index pairing assumes fronts and backs have equal lengths.
Complexity: Building the set and scanning both lists take O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees whose internal nodes multiply two child values to equal the parent, using the supplied values.
Idea: Memoize the number of trees rooted at each value and try every value as a possible factor.
Technique and why it applies: Each value starts with one single-node tree. For every factor pair present in the set, multiply the number of left and right subtree choices and add them.
Invariant: helper(num) counts trees rooted at num, including the single-node tree.
Edge cases: lru_cache is used without being imported. Iterating all factors includes both factor orders, which is appropriate for ordered left/right children but requires the input's positive distinct values.
Complexity: With n values, memoized factor checks take O(n²) time and O(n) cached states, excluding recursive stack depth.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees where each non-leaf parent equals the product of its two children, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sort values and compute the number of trees rooted at each value using smaller factors.
Technique and why it applies: Each value begins with one single-node tree. Every factor A[j] divides A[i], and a complementary factor already computed, contributes the product of their tree counts.
Invariant: dp[x] stores the number of valid trees whose root value is x.
Edge cases: A is sorted in place. The method assumes distinct positive values and uses the modulo after each addition to control integer growth.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Convert each word in a sentence to Goat Latin, adding ma and a progressively longer suffix.
Idea: Split the sentence into words, move an initial consonant to the end when needed, and append the required suffix.
Technique and why it applies: Vowel-starting words stay in place; other words rotate their first character to the end. Word index determines the number of trailing a characters.
Invariant: index is the one-based word position and result accumulates converted words separated by spaces.
Edge cases: sentence.split(' ') preserves empty tokens from repeated spaces, which can cause word[0] to fail. The usual input has single spaces between nonempty words.
Complexity: The conversion is O(n) in total sentence length, though repeated string concatenation may add copying overhead.

Task and constraints: Convert a sentence to Goat Latin by applying a word transformation and appending an index-dependent suffix.
Idea: Iterate over whitespace-separated words, transform consonant-starting words, and yield each converted word.
Technique and why it applies: The generator moves the first character of a consonant-starting word to its end, then appends ma and i copies of a.
Invariant: The generator yields each transformed word in original order, with i beginning at one.
Edge cases: split() collapses repeated whitespace and ignores leading/trailing whitespace, unlike split(' '). Empty sentences yield an empty output string.
Complexity: Processing is linear in input and output size, with O(n) output storage.

Task and constraints: Count directed friend requests among people using age-based eligibility rules.
Idea: Count people by age and evaluate each ordered pair of distinct people by age category.
Technique and why it applies: request(a,b) expresses the permitted age inequality. Multiplying the two age frequencies counts all pairings, and subtracting one when ages match prevents each person requesting themselves.
Invariant: c[a] records how many people have age a, and the double sum counts eligible directed pairs.
Edge cases: The helper's rule is a simplified eligibility condition and should match the full problem restrictions. If a==b, c[b]-1 excludes self-pairing.
Complexity: For U distinct ages, time is O(U²+n) and space is O(U).

Task and constraints: Maximize total profit by assigning each worker at most one job they can perform.
Idea: Sort jobs by difficulty, build prefix maximum profits, and binary-search the hardest feasible job for each worker.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix maxima ensure the chosen difficulty position also represents the best profit among all easier jobs.
Invariant: arr[j][1] is the maximum profit among jobs with difficulty no greater than arr[j][0].
Edge cases: The snippet uses inf without importing or defining it, so it raises NameError. Workers unable to do any job earn zero.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), prefix processing O(n), and each of m workers searches in O(log n), matching O(n log n + m log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest island obtainable by changing at most one water cell into land.
Idea: Use disjoint-set union to connect neighboring land cells and store each component's size.
Technique and why it applies: For each water cell, gather distinct neighboring component roots and sum their sizes plus one for the flipped cell.
Invariant: parent identifies land components and rank stores component sizes, with water initialized to size zero.
Edge cases: The index expression uses i*m+j instead of i*n+j; this is wrong for rectangular grids. The supplied code also appears to have inconsistent indentation before the neighbor-index logic, which may prevent parsing.
Complexity: With correct indexing, DSU operations are near-linear and space is O(mn); as written, rectangular cases are incorrect.

Task and constraints: Find the largest island after optionally changing one zero to one.
Idea: Label each existing island with DFS and store its area, then test every zero by summing distinct adjacent island areas.
Technique and why it applies: Recoloring visited land with a unique index prevents revisits. A set avoids counting the same island more than once when it touches the flipped cell from multiple sides.
Invariant: area[index] is the size of the island labeled with that index in grid.
Edge cases: If the grid is all land, the initial maximum returns its area. If all water, flipping one cell yields one; the code handles this with the default [0] area list.
Complexity: DFS labels every cell once and each zero checks four neighbors, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) storage.

Task and constraints: Sum the number of substrings in which each character contributes when it appears exactly once.
Idea: Record each character's occurrence indices and count substrings where each occurrence is unique.
Technique and why it applies: For occurrence i, the nearest same-character positions on either side delimit the possible start/end choices. Multiplying the left and right distances counts substrings where this occurrence is the only copy.
Invariant: idx_recorder[c] stores all indices where character c appears.
Edge cases: collections is used without importing it in the snippet. The helper resets its local ans and the outer function sums each character's contribution.
Complexity: Building occurrence lists and summing contributions take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the sum of unique-character counts over every substring, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Track the previous two occurrence positions of each uppercase letter and add each occurrence's contribution when encountered.
Technique and why it applies: If a character last appeared at k and before that at j, its contribution for the current occurrence is (i-j)*(j-k), counting substrings where this occurrence is the unique copy.
Invariant: index[c] stores the two most recent positions of c, initialized to -1.
Edge cases: The algorithm assumes uppercase English letters because it iterates string.ascii_uppercase. The final pass accounts for substrings extending to the end after each character's last occurrence.
Complexity: Two passes over the fixed alphabet and string take O(n+Σ) time and O(Σ) space, with Σ=26.

Task and constraints: Count ways to express positive integer n as a sum of one or more consecutive positive integers.
Idea: Consider each possible sequence length i and track the triangular offset before its first term.
Technique and why it applies: A length-i sequence beginning at x sums to i*x + i(i-1)/2. The accumulated csum is that offset; divisibility of n-csum by i determines whether x is an integer.
Invariant: csum equals 0+1+...+(i-1) for the current length i.
Edge cases: The loop stops once csum reaches n because longer lengths cannot yield a positive starting value. n is assumed positive.
Complexity: The loop runs O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return start and end indices for each run of at least three identical consecutive characters.
Idea: Scan the string while maintaining the current run length and previous character.
Technique and why it applies: When a character changes, the previous run is complete and is emitted if its length is at least three. A final check handles a qualifying run ending at the last character.
Invariant: c counts the current run's length and prev stores its repeated character.
Edge cases: The final-run condition uses bitwise & instead of logical and; for boolean operands it still evaluates both sides but gives a truthy integer result. Empty strings return an empty list.
Complexity: One scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond results.

Task and constraints: Find all intervals representing groups of three or more identical adjacent characters.
Idea: Track the beginning of each run and close it when the character changes or the string ends.
Technique and why it applies: At each run boundary, j-i+1 gives the run length; qualifying ranges are appended with inclusive endpoints.
Invariant: i marks the first index of the current run.
Edge cases: The boundary condition short-circuits at the last index, so S[j+1] is never accessed out of range. Empty input returns an empty result.
Complexity: A single pass takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space apart from output.

Task and constraints: Mask an email address or phone number according to personal-information masking rules.
Idea: Branch on whether the input contains @; lowercase and mask email names, otherwise strip phone formatting and preserve only masked digits.
Technique and why it applies: Email output keeps the first and last local-part letters with five stars. Phone processing scans right to left, inserts separators and stars, and adds a country prefix based on extra digits.
Invariant: res is assembled as characters are processed, while l counts digits and flag switches from visible local digits to masking.
Edge cases: The email branch assumes exactly two @-separated pieces and at least two domain labels. Phone formatting logic relies on exact lengths and is fragile for unusual inputs.
Complexity: Both branches scan O(n) characters and use O(n) output storage.

Task and constraints: Reverse each row of a binary image and invert every bit.
Idea: Use a nested list comprehension that reverses each row and maps each bit to 1 minus itself.
Technique and why it applies: Reversal handles the horizontal flip, and 1-i swaps zero and one.
Invariant: Each output row contains the inverted values from the corresponding input row in reverse order.
Edge cases: The input image is not modified; empty images and empty rows produce corresponding empty structures.
Complexity: Every cell is visited once, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) output space.

Task and constraints: Flip every row horizontally and invert its binary values in place.
Idea: Swap symmetric elements while XOR-inverting both values.
Technique and why it applies: XOR with one flips a binary bit. Pairwise swaps reverse the row, and processing through the midpoint also handles the center element of odd-length rows.
Invariant: After each pair operation, the processed outer positions contain inverted values from their opposite original positions.
Edge cases: The method mutates and returns A. The midpoint loop includes the center for odd lengths, where both assignments target the same element but still invert it once.
Complexity: Each cell is processed a constant number of times, giving O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Apply multiple replacements to s at specified original indices when the corresponding source text matches.
Idea: Sort replacement operations by index and adjust later indices as earlier replacements change string length.
Technique and why it applies: offset accumulates the net length difference from prior successful replacements, translating original indices into current-string positions.
Invariant: offset equals the total length change caused by successful replacements already applied.
Edge cases: The code prints debug messages for failed matches. It processes replacements left to right and uses the adjusted index against the already modified string, which can be error-prone when operations overlap.
Complexity: Sorting is O(k log k), while each string slice/concatenation can cost O(n), yielding O(kn) worst-case time and O(n) string storage.

Task and constraints: Apply all specified find-and-replace operations using original indices and only when source text matches.
Idea: Sort operations by decreasing index so replacements to the right do not shift indices to the left.
Technique and why it applies: Each operation checks the source substring at its original position, then replaces it. Descending order keeps all earlier positions valid despite changes in suffix lengths.
Invariant: Before processing index i, all already-applied operations are strictly to its right, so the prefix through i is unchanged.
Edge cases: A failed source match is skipped. Equal indices are not expected; reverse sorting determines their order if present.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(k log k), and repeated string slicing can take O(kn) time with O(n) space per replacement.
